newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Chechen catastrophe feared as aid workers pull out.
newsitem.headline: Chechen catastrophe feared as aid workers pull out.

text.p: Doctors said on Wednesday that thousands of Chechens might get no medical treatment now that foreign aid organisations were pulling out of the rebel Russian region and one said she feared a catastrophe.
Most international aid agencies were pulling out of Chechnya after six workers of the International Committee of the Red Cross were murdered there on Tuesday.

"It will be a big catastrophe for us. We just don't have the resources to help people," said Lyuba Archakova, head doctor in City Hospital 4 in the capital Grozny. "The foreign aid organisations were bringing us all our equipment and medicine."
The six workers -- five women and a man -- were killed by masked gunmen as they slept in a Red Cross hospital compound in the village of Novye Atagi.
The Red Cross said on Tuesday it was withdrawing all its international staff, leaving local staff to look after the Novye Atagi hospital and other Chechnya relief offices.

Some Chechens may be able to afford medical care if they have relatives sending money from Russia or abroad, but Bertrand Kern, deputy head of the Red Cross in Moscow said many would have nowhere to turn without international aid.
"There will be a large number -- I would say thousands of people -- who will be left with virtually no resources," he said. "There is a high risk that these people will just die."

He said the Red Cross aid effort, by far the largest international aid programme to Chechnya, was worth roughly $25 million in 1996. It funded hospitals as well as sanitation programmes to help get clean water to local people.
"Without water, without minimum hygenic conditions, the risk is very high that people will just not survive," he said.
On Wednesday, the French aid organisation Medecins sans Frontieres said it was suspending its Chechnya mission in solidarity. Other organisations have followed suit.

The foreign aid is vital in institutions such as Clinical Hospital 1 in Grozny, where the doctors huddle together in the building's only room with glass in the windows. There is no running water anywhere.

"Children are coming in and they can't get treated because we don't have enough medicine," said Lyalya Eskayeva, deputy head director. "We just can't take money from people because of the overall situation."

At City Hospital 4, children who play in the ruins of the capital are often wounded by the remnants of bullets and explosives left from nearly two years of fighting between separatist rebels and the Russian army.
"Last year we treated 1,000 sick children. This year we already saw more than that in the first six months of the year," said Archakova.
Chechen separatists said on Tuesday the murder was carried out by professionals who broke into the hospital and apparently used silenced guns.
It was the worst single assault on Red Cross workers and the bloodiest incident involving foreigners on Russian soil for many years.
